newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: ANALYSIS - Australian oppn suffers in Colston affair.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSIS - Australian oppn suffers in Colston affair.

text.p: Australia's Labor opposition is beginning to take a share of the political damage from the accusations of expenses fraud against key independent senator Mal Colston.

The most serious issue remains the risk that Colston, whose vote is crucial for government legislation, might have to quit the Senate if convicted for his alleged false claims of travelling allowance and other entitlements.

But talkback radio, letters to newspapers and opinion polls suggest voters are riotously unhappy about politicians abusing perks and blame the government for not immediately calling in the police on Colston, who denies the allegations.
Now the Liberal-National government is deflecting that blame onto Labor -- the party Colston represented for 21 years before defecting last year -- as old accusations against him have emerged.

"The truth of the matter is the Labor government repeatedly failed to take correct decisions on advice tendered to them and on specific recommendations tendered to them," Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer told reporters on Friday.
The Australian newspaper on Friday reported that Colston had twice been forced to refund overclaimed expenses in the early 1980s, when he was a Labor senator.
Callers castigated Labor leader Kim Beazley when he appeared on talkback radio on Thursday.

"I know unionists who are disgusted by this that for basically 15 to 16 years Labor has supported this man in power," one man told Beazley. "You guys knew what he was like and you didn't get rid of him."

Allegations against Colston surfaced in February but Prime Minister John Howard declined to call in the police until Tuesday, when Colston's secretary retracted a statement in which she had taken the blame for false expense claims.

Howard also said Colston should also step down as deputy Senate president, a job with which he was rewarded when he quit the Labor Party in August. "I'm sure he'll be gone as deputy president before the Senate resumes (in May) and if he's not we'll vote him out," he said on Friday.
Before Labor came under fire for its treatment of Colston, the government's opinion poll standing -- always volatile -- tended to slip, one poll showing Howard's lead falling six percentage points.
But the government's slow handling of Colston's affairs was not the only factor that may have affected voters in that time.
Last month federal parliament overturned a pioneering euthanasia law enacted by one of Australia's territories.
The federal move outraged the 70 percent of voters polled who thought the terminally ill should be allowed to kill themselves.
No polls have measured the position since the emergence of allegations of earlier misbehaviour by Colston.
The government has not wanted to lose Colston because it is two votes short of a majority in the Senate, the upper house.

Since he defected, Colston and another independent senator have routinely supplied those two votes, letting the government enact severe budget cuts and authorising the sale of telecoms carrier Telstra Corp AOT.AX.
The Liberal-National government was elected in March 1996, ending 13 years of Labor rule.
